Third Use of the Law
thurd yoos uhv thuh law
doctrinal phrase
From the threefold division of the law’s uses; the “third use” (Latin tertius usus legis) is its function as a rule of life for the believer.

Biblical Definition

The third use of the law is its function as a rule of life for the believer—the moral law, summed in the Ten Commandments and the two great commandments, serving the regenerate as the guide and standard of grateful obedience. The Reformed tradition distinguishes three uses of the moral law: the first, or civil use, restrains sin in society; the second, or pedagogical use, convicts of sin and drives the sinner to Christ as a schoolmaster; and the third, or normative use, directs the believer in the way he should walk. This third use is the chief use of the law for the Christian. Though he is no longer under the law as a covenant of works for his justification, having been freed from its curse by Christ, the believer is not without law to God but under the law to Christ, and he delights in the law of God after the inward man. The law cannot justify him, but it shows him the will of God and the path of holiness; freed from its condemnation, he is now free to love and obey it as a son, not a slave. The dictionary holds the third use of the law as the answer to antinomianism, which casts off the law as a rule of life under the pretense of grace. Grace does not abolish the moral law but establishes it, writing it on the heart in the new covenant, so that the justified believer obeys not to earn favor but out of love and gratitude for favor already received. The law, no longer a covenant of works, remains the believer’s rule, his delight, and the Spirit-empowered pattern of his sanctification.

Webster 1828 Definition

The moral law’s function as the believer’s rule of life—not for justification, from whose curse he is freed, but as the guide of grateful, Spirit-empowered obedience; the answer to antinomianism.

THIRD USE OF THE LAW, the moral law as the believer’s rule of life.

Distinguished from the civil use (restraining sin) and the pedagogical use (driving to Christ).

The chief use of the law for the Christian.

Not under the law for justification, yet under the law to Christ as a rule.

The answer to antinomianism, which casts off the law as a rule of life.

Key Scripture

Psa 119:97 — "O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day."

Rom 7:22 — "For I delight in the law of God after the inward man:"

1Co 9:21 — "To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law."

Rom 8:4 — "That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

Modern Corruption

Antinomianism casts off the moral law as a rule of life, mistaking freedom from the law’s curse for freedom from its guidance.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the third use of the law against antinomianism. The believer is freed from the law as a covenant of works and from its curse, justified by faith apart from works; but he is not therefore without law to God. He is under the law to Christ, delights in the law of God after the inward man, and walks after the Spirit that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in him. To cast off the moral law as a rule of life, under the pretense of grace, is the antinomian error grace itself condemns.

The doctrine must be guarded equally from legalism on the other side, which puts the believer back under the law as a covenant of works and makes obedience the ground of acceptance. The dictionary holds the Reformed balance. The law cannot justify, and the believer’s standing rests wholly on Christ’s imputed righteousness received by faith; yet the same grace that justifies also writes the law on the heart and sanctifies, so that the believer obeys not to earn favor but out of gratitude for favor freely given. Grace does not abolish the moral law but establishes it. The law remains the believer’s rule, his delight, and the Spirit-empowered pattern of his growing holiness.

Hebrew Roots

The phrase names the law’s use as the believer’s rule of life—a guide to grateful obedience, not a covenant of works.

Latin tertius usus legis — the third use of the law.

The first use: civil, restraining sin in society.

The second use: pedagogical, convicting and driving to Christ.

The third use: normative, the believer’s rule of life.

The chief use of the moral law for the Christian.

Usage

"The third use of the law is the moral law as the believer’s rule of grateful obedience."

"It is the Reformed answer to antinomianism."

"It is held with justification by faith against legalism on the other side."
